The Iceland project has been increased in scale and is set to store 10,000 tonnes of CO2 a year.

So they're injecting a CO2-rich water solution (carbonated water, basically) into hot basalt structures, and it's catalytically locking the carbon up into the rock structure. Nice! Not only is it being returned directly to an existing natural state, but it seems like we can do it at large scales.

Even more promising is the ocean floor, which is full of basalt and a good place to store the carbon dioxide, said Dr Goldberg.

Clever! Like most carbon-capture methods it's expensive, but any time you try to handle bulk chemicals without an end product to sell you're going to be spending money. I'm curious if their CO2 came as expensive liquid supply or if they were collecting it with bulk impurities from a waste stream somehow.
